questions.question: Which of the following conditions is routinely included in the newborn screening panel in India as per the National Health Portal guidelines?

options.text: Cystic fibrosis
options.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is not included in the standard Indian newborn screening panel.

options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
options.explanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is mandated for screening in India.

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
options.explanation: G6PD deficiency is screened in some states but not universally mandated.

options.text: Maple syrup urine disease
options.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease is not included in the standard Indian screening panel.

questions.explanation: India’s newborn screening program mandates testing for congenital adrenal hyperplasia as per the National Health Portal guidelines. While G6PD deficiency is also screened in some states, it is not universally mandated. Cystic fibrosis and maple syrup urine disease are not included in the standard Indian screening panel.
questions.hint: Consider conditions with mandatory screening in India.

questions.question: A 38-week gestation newborn presents with vomiting, hypoglycemia, and ambiguous genitalia on day 3 of life. Which metabolic disorder should be suspected and screened for immediately?

options.text: Phenylketonuria
options.explanation: Phenylketonuria does not present with ambiguous genitalia or hypoglycemia.

options.text: Maple syrup urine disease
options.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease presents with neurological symptoms, not ambiguous genitalia.

options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
options.explanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia presents with vomiting, hypoglycemia, and ambiguous genitalia.

options.text: Tyrosinemia
options.explanation: Tyrosinemia does not present with ambiguous genitalia.

questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of vomiting, hypoglycemia, and ambiguous genitalia is classic for congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Immediate screening for serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone is indicated. The other options do not present with ambiguous genitalia.
questions.hint: Look for symptoms of adrenal insufficiency and ambiguous genitalia.
questions.subject: norcet-obg

questions.question: A preterm neonate (32 weeks) is on day 7 of life. The nurse notes yellowish discoloration of the skin starting from the face and progressing downward. Total serum bilirubin is 12 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management according to AAP guidelines?

options.text: Start phototherapy immediately
options.explanation: Phototherapy is indicated for bilirubin levels of 12 mg/dL in preterm infants.

options.text: Perform exchange transfusion
options.explanation: Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin levels ≥18–20 mg/dL or acute bilirubin encephalopathy.

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin
options.explanation: IV immunoglobulin is not a primary treatment for hyperbilirubinemia.

options.text: Increase oral feeding frequency
options.explanation: Increasing feeding frequency is not a primary treatment for hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.explanation: According to the AAP (2004) guidelines, phototherapy is indicated when total serum bilirubin reaches 12 mg/dL in preterm infants aged 7 days. Exchange transfusion is reserved for levels ≥18–20 mg/dL or in cases of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. IV immunoglobulin and increased feeding are not primary treatments for hyperbilirubinemia.
questions.hint: Refer to AAP guidelines for bilirubin management in preterm infants.
questions.subject: norcet-obg

questions.question: A 2-day-old term newborn is found to have a positive screen for phenylketonuria (PKU) with plasma phenylalanine level of 20 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start a phenylalanine-restricted diet immediately
options.explanation: A phenylalanine-restricted diet is essential to prevent neurological damage in PKU.

options.text: Repeat the test after 48 hours
options.explanation: Repeating the test is not appropriate when levels are already diagnostic.

options.text: Begin phenylalanine supplementation
options.explanation: Phenylalanine supplementation is contraindicated in PKU.

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium benzoate
options.explanation: Sodium benzoate is used in urea cycle disorders, not PKU.

questions.explanation: A plasma phenylalanine level ≥15–20 mg/dL in a 2-day-old newborn confirms PKU. Immediate dietary restriction of phenylalanine is essential to prevent neurological damage. Repeating the test or supplementation is inappropriate at this stage. Sodium benzoate is used in urea cycle disorders, not PKU.
questions.hint: Consider immediate dietary intervention for PKU.
questions.subject: norcet-obg

questions.question: Which of the following newborn screening test results would prompt an urgent referral to a pediatric endocrinologist?

options.text: TSH level of 20 mIU/L
options.explanation: TSH ≥20 mIU/L indicates congenital hypothyroidism and requires urgent referral.

options.text: Galactose level of 4 mg/dL
options.explanation: Galactose 4 mg/dL is within normal limits.

options.text: Hemoglobin A1c of 5.8%
options.explanation: Hemoglobin A1c is not part of newborn screening.

options.text: Serum calcium of 8.5 mg/dL
options.explanation: Serum calcium is not part of newborn screening.

questions.explanation: A TSH level ≥20 mIU/L is diagnostic of congenital hypothyroidism and requires urgent endocrine referral to prevent intellectual disability. Galactose 4 mg/dL is within normal limits. Hemoglobin A1c and calcium levels are not part of newborn screening panels.
questions.hint: Identify the condition requiring urgent endocrine referral.
questions.subject: norcet-obg

questions.question: A 5-hour-old term newborn is found to have a positive screen for medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency. The parents are consanguineous. What is the most critical counseling point for the parents regarding feeding?

options.text: Feed every 2 hours to prevent hypoglycemia
options.explanation: Frequent feeding is essential to prevent hypoglycemia in MCAD deficiency.

options.text: Use a high-protein formula
options.explanation: High-protein formula is not a standard recommendation for MCAD deficiency.

options.text: Delay breastfeeding for 48 hours
options.explanation: Delaying breastfeeding is not recommended in MCAD deficiency.

options.text: Add medium-chain triglyceride oil to feeds
options.explanation: MCT oil supplementation is not a standard recommendation for MCAD deficiency.

questions.explanation: In MCAD deficiency, fasting can precipitate hypoglycemia and metabolic crises. Frequent feeding (every 2–3 hours) is essential to prevent hypoglycemia. High-protein formula, delayed breastfeeding, or MCT oil supplementation are not standard recommendations; avoidance of fasting is key.
questions.hint: Focus on preventing hypoglycemia in MCAD deficiency.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is NOT typically included in the recommended uniform screening panel (RUSP) for newborns in the United States?

options.text: Sickle cell disease
options.explanation: Sickle cell disease is included in the RUSP.

options.text: Congenital hypothyroidism
options.explanation: Congenital hypothyroidism is included in the RUSP.

options.text: Spinal muscular atrophy
options.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy is included in the RUSP.

options.text: Cystic fibrosis
options.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is included in the RUSP, so this is incorrect.

questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is included in the RUSP. Spinal muscular atrophy was added to the RUSP in 2018. Sickle cell disease and congenital hypothyroidism have been part of the panel for decades.
questions.hint: Identify the condition not included in the RUSP.

questions.question: A newborn screening report shows a positive result for galactosemia. The nurse notes that the baby is exclusively breastfed. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Switch to lactose-free formula
options.explanation: Lactose-free formula must be started immediately to prevent complications in galactosemia.

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and monitor for jaundice
options.explanation: Continuing breastfeeding is contraindicated in galactosemia.

options.text: Administer intravenous galactose
options.explanation: Administering galactose is contraindicated in galactosemia.

options.text: Perform a liver biopsy
options.explanation: Liver biopsy is not indicated in the initial management of galactosemia.

questions.explanation: In galactosemia, lactose-containing feeds (breast milk or standard formula) must be discontinued immediately, and lactose-free formula should be started to prevent liver damage, cataracts, and sepsis. Continuing breastfeeding or administering galactose is contraindicated. Liver biopsy is not indicated at this stage.
questions.hint: Discontinue lactose-containing feeds immediately in galactosemia.

questions.question: A 10-day-old infant presents with poor feeding, lethargy, and a positive screen for maple syrup urine disease (MSUD). The urine has a characteristic 'maple syrup' odor. Which amino acid is elevated in plasma that confirms the diagnosis?

options.text: Leucine
options.explanation: Leucine is the primary amino acid elevated in MSUD.

options.text: Tyrosine
options.explanation: Tyrosine is not elevated in MSUD.

options.text: Phenylalanine
options.explanation: Phenylalanine is not elevated in MSUD.

options.text: Valine
options.explanation: Valine is elevated but not the primary diagnostic amino acid in MSUD.

questions.explanation: MSUD is characterized by elevated branched-chain amino acids, primarily leucine, with secondary elevations in valine and isoleucine. Tyrosine and phenylalanine are not elevated in MSUD. The 'maple syrup' odor is due to accumulation of these branched-chain amino acids.
questions.hint: Identify the amino acid elevated in MSUD.

questions.question: A preterm infant (34 weeks) is discharged from the NICU on day 21 of life. The newborn screening report shows a borderline elevation in 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the newborn screen in 2–4 weeks
options.explanation: A repeat screen is necessary to confirm or rule out congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

options.text: Immediately start hydrocortisone therapy
options.explanation: Immediate therapy is not indicated unless levels are significantly elevated.

options.text: Refer to a pediatric surgeon
options.explanation: Surgery is not relevant in this context.

options.text: Perform a karyotype analysis
options.explanation: Karyotype analysis is not indicated for borderline 17-hydroxyprogesterone elevations.

questions.explanation: Borderline elevations in 17-hydroxyprogesterone require a repeat screen to confirm or rule out congenital adrenal hyperplasia, as false positives can occur due to prematurity or stress. Immediate therapy is not indicated unless levels are significantly elevated. Karyotype and surgery are not relevant in this context.
questions.hint: Consider repeating the screening test for borderline elevations.

questions.question: When is the initial newborn screening typically performed in a healthy term infant?

options.text: Within 12 hours of birth
options.explanation: Screening within 12 hours is too early for accurate metabolic detection.

options.text: Between 24 and 48 hours of age
options.explanation: Correct. This timing allows for metabolic adaptation while ensuring early detection.

options.text: At 7 days of life
options.explanation: Screening at 7 days is too late and may delay treatment.

options.text: Before hospital discharge regardless of age
options.explanation: Discharge before 24 hours may lead to inaccurate results.

questions.explanation: Newborn screening is ideally done after 24 hours of life to allow for the metabolism of certain compounds; however, it must occur before 48 hours to ensure early detection and treatment of disorders.
questions.hint: Screening should occur after metabolic adaptation but before discharge.

questions.question: Which metabolic disorder is detected by measuring phenylalanine levels in the newborn screening test?

options.text: Maple Syrup Urine Disease
options.explanation: MSUD is detected by elevated leucine, isoleucine, and valine levels.

options.text: Homocystinuria
options.explanation: Homocystinuria involves elevated homocysteine and methionine levels.

options.text: Phenylketonuria
options.explanation: Correct. PKU is detected by elevated phenylalanine levels.

options.text: Tyrosinemia
options.explanation: Tyrosinemia involves elevated tyrosine levels.

questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is characterized by elevated phenylalanine levels due to a deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, which is detected via newborn screening.
questions.hint: Think of disorders related to amino acid metabolism.

questions.question: A newborn is discharged at 36 hours of life without undergoing newborn screening. What is the most appropriate next step for the healthcare provider?

options.text: Perform the test immediately upon the next visit
options.explanation: Immediate testing is not necessary; 3–5 days is sufficient.

options.text: Schedule the test within 3–5 days of life
options.explanation: Correct. This ensures timely detection without unnecessary delay.

options.text: Defer testing as the infant is already discharged
options.explanation: Deferring testing may lead to delayed diagnosis and treatment.

options.text: Wait until the infant shows symptoms before testing
options.explanation: Waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of early screening.

questions.explanation: If newborn screening is missed before 48 hours, it should be performed within 3–5 days of life to ensure timely detection of disorders while avoiding unnecessary delay.
questions.hint: Consider the timing for accurate metabolic detection in missed cases.

options.text: Cystic Fibrosis

options.text: Sickle Cell Disease

options.text: Congenital Hypothyroidism

options.text: Down Syndrome

questions.explanation: Down Syndrome is not part of the RUSP; the panel includes conditions like cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, and congenital hypothyroidism due to their significant health impact and effective early interventions.

questions.question: A 3-day-old term infant presents with poor feeding and lethargy. The newborn screening report shows elevated leucine levels. Which condition is most likely responsible?

options.text: Tyrosinemia
options.explanation: Tyrosinemia involves elevated tyrosine levels, not leucine.

options.text: Isovaleric Acidemia
options.explanation: Isovaleric acidemia involves elevated isovaleric acid, not leucine.

options.text: Maple Syrup Urine Disease
options.explanation: Correct. MSUD is characterized by elevated leucine levels.

options.text: Organic Acidemia
options.explanation: Organic acidemia is a general term and not specific to elevated leucine.

questions.explanation: Elevated leucine levels are indicative of Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD), an amino acid disorder characterized by the inability to metabolize branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine).
questions.hint: Consider disorders related to branched-chain amino acid metabolism.

questions.question: Calculate the expected weight loss percentage for a term infant on Day 3 of life who weighed 3.2 kg at birth and now weighs 2.95 kg.

options.explanation: Incorrect calculation. The correct percentage is 7.81%.
Correct. The calculation matches the expected weight loss percentage.
Incorrect calculation. The correct percentage is 7.81%.
Incorrect calculation. The correct percentage is 7.81%.

questions.explanation: Weight loss = (Birth weight - Current weight) / Birth weight × 100 = (3.2 - 2.95) / 3.2 × 100 = 0.25 / 3.2 × 100 = 7.81%. This falls within the normal range of 5–10% weight loss in the first few days of life.
questions.hint: Use the formula for weight loss percentage: (Initial weight - Current weight) / Initial weight × 100.

questions.question: Which of the following newborn screening results indicates a need for immediate follow-up and possible emergency treatment?

options.text: Borderline elevated bilirubin
options.explanation: Borderline bilirubin elevation does not typically require immediate emergency treatment.

options.text: Positive result for congenital adrenal hyperplasia
options.explanation: Correct. CAH requires immediate intervention to prevent adrenal crisis.

options.text: Mild elevation in thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
options.explanation: Mild TSH elevation may require follow-up but not immediate emergency treatment.

options.text: Low methionine levels
options.explanation: Low methionine levels do not typically require immediate emergency treatment.

questions.explanation: A positive result for congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) requires immediate intervention to prevent life-threatening adrenal crisis, making it a critical condition detected by newborn screening.

questions.question: A preterm infant born at 35 weeks gestation is discharged at 10 days of life. When should the newborn screening be performed?

options.text: Within 48 hours of birth
options.explanation: Screening within 48 hours may not account for metabolic immaturity in preterm infants.

options.text: At 7–14 days of corrected age
options.explanation: Correct. This timing accounts for physiological immaturity in preterm infants.

options.text: On the day of discharge
options.explanation: Discharge timing may not align with metabolic adaptation in preterm infants.

options.text: Only if the infant shows symptoms
options.explanation: Waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of early screening.

questions.explanation: For preterm infants, newborn screening should be done at 7–14 days of corrected age to account for physiological immaturity and delayed metabolic adaptation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary goal of newborn screening programs?

options.text: To identify genetic disorders before symptoms appear
options.explanation: Correct. Early detection allows for timely intervention and improved outcomes.

options.text: To confirm diagnoses of common childhood infections
options.explanation: Newborn screening does not focus on childhood infections.

options.text: To monitor growth and development trends
options.explanation: Monitoring growth and development is not the primary goal of newborn screening.

options.text: To reduce hospital readmission rates
options.explanation: Reducing readmission rates is not the primary goal of newborn screening.

questions.explanation: The primary goal of newborn screening is early detection of serious but treatable conditions before symptoms develop, allowing for timely intervention and improved outcomes.

questions.question: A newborn screening report indicates a positive result for galactosemia. Which dietary intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Immediate initiation of a phenylalanine-restricted diet
options.explanation: A phenylalanine-restricted diet is for phenylketonuria, not galactosemia.

options.text: Avoidance of lactose-containing formulas and breast milk
options.explanation: Correct. Galactosemia requires strict avoidance of lactose.

options.text: Supplementation with vitamin K
options.explanation: Vitamin K supplementation is not the primary treatment for galactosemia.

options.text: Administration of phenobarbital
options.explanation: Phenobarbital is not a treatment for galactosemia.

questions.explanation: Galactosemia is an inability to metabolize galactose, a sugar found in milk. The primary treatment is strict avoidance of lactose-containing foods, including breast milk and most formulas.
questions.hint: Consider the metabolic defect in galactosemia and its dietary implications.

questions.question: A 2-day-old term neonate has passed meconium but is exclusively breastfed. The nurse observes the infant has not voided in the last 24 hours. Which of the following is the MOST likely explanation for this finding?

options.text: Dehydration secondary to inadequate breastfeeding
options.explanation: Dehydration is less likely without signs of inadequate intake such as sunken fontanelle or poor latch.

options.text: Normal physiological oliguria in the first 48 hours of life
options.explanation: Reduced urine output in the first 48 hours is a normal physiological finding during the transition from fetal to neonatal renal function.

options.text: Congenital renal anomaly such as bilateral renal agenesis
options.explanation: Congenital renal anomalies are rare and typically accompanied by other systemic signs.

options.text: Delayed transition from fetal to neonatal renal function
options.explanation: Delayed renal transition is not a recognized clinical entity.

questions.explanation: In the first 48 hours of life, it is normal for neonates to have reduced urine output as they transition from the fluid-rich intrauterine environment to independent renal function. Breastfed infants may have fewer wet diapers in the first two days. While dehydration (A) is a consideration, it is less likely without signs of inadequate intake (e.g., sunken fontanelle, poor latch). Congenital anomalies (C) are rare and typically accompanied by other systemic signs. Delayed renal transition (D) is not a recognized clinical entity.
questions.hint: Consider normal physiological changes in the first 48 hours of life.

questions.question: During a home visit on Day 3 postpartum, a community nurse assesses a newborn who weighed 3.2 kg at birth. The current weight is 3.0 kg. The mother reports the infant has fed well 8–10 times in 24 hours. Which of the following BEST explains the weight loss?

options.text: Sepsis with poor oral intake
options.explanation: Sepsis is unlikely given the infant’s adequate feeding pattern.

options.text: Physiological weight loss of 6–8% from birth weight
options.explanation: A 6.25% weight loss is within the normal physiological range for the first few days of life.

options.text: Congenital heart disease causing fluid overload
options.explanation: Congenital heart disease is not supported by the clinical picture.

options.text: Maternal diabetes leading to neonatal hyperglycemia
options.explanation: Maternal diabetes is not indicated by the clinical findings.

questions.explanation: Physiological weight loss of 5–10% in the first 3–5 days is normal due to fluid shifts and limited intake immediately after birth. A 6.25% loss (0.2 kg from 3.2 kg) falls within this range. The infant’s feeding pattern is adequate, making sepsis unlikely. Congenital heart disease (C) and maternal diabetes (D) are not supported by the clinical picture.
questions.hint: Consider normal physiological changes in the first few days of life.
questions.subject: norcet-obg

questions.question: A preterm infant (34 weeks) is admitted to the NICU and scheduled for newborn screening (NBS). The nurse notes the following lab values from cord blood: TSH 12 mIU/L, T4 8 µg/dL. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat TSH and T4 in 48 hours
options.explanation: Repeating tests unnecessarily delays treatment for congenital hypothyroidism.

options.text: Initiate levothyroxine therapy immediately
options.explanation: Immediate levothyroxine therapy is indicated to prevent neurodevelopmental delay in congenital hypothyroidism.

options.text: Perform a hearing screen before NBS
options.explanation: Hearing screen is important but secondary to treating hypothyroidism.

options.text: Wait for the NBS report before acting
options.explanation: Waiting risks delayed treatment for congenital hypothyroidism.

questions.explanation: Normal TSH is <10 mIU/L and T4 >10 µg/dL in term infants; preterm values are higher due to immaturity. However, TSH >10 mIU/L with low T4 in a preterm infant warrants concern for congenital hypothyroidism. Immediate levothyroxine therapy is indicated to prevent neurodevelopmental delay. Waiting (D) risks delayed treatment. A repeat test (A) is unnecessary delay. Hearing screen (C) is important but secondary to treating hypothyroidism.
questions.hint: Consider the significance of TSH and T4 levels in preterm infants.

questions.question: A 7-day-old exclusively breastfed infant presents with jaundice. Total serum bilirubin is 18 mg/dL, with direct bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL. The infant is breastfeeding well, has normal urine output, and no signs of kernicterus. Which of the following is the BEST next intervention?

options.text: Discontinue breastfeeding and switch to formula
options.explanation: Discontinuing breastfeeding is not indicated unless there is evidence of dehydration or poor intake.

options.text: Administer IV immunoglobulin
options.explanation: IVIG is used for isoimmune hemolysis, which is not indicated in this case.

options.text: Begin intensive phototherapy
options.explanation: Intensive phototherapy is the first-line treatment for a bilirubin level of 18 mg/dL in a 7-day-old term infant.

options.text: Order an abdominal ultrasound for biliary atresia
options.explanation: An ultrasound is premature without evidence of cholestasis or other risk factors.

questions.explanation: The bilirubin level of 18 mg/dL in a 7-day-old term infant falls into the high-intermediate risk zone per AAP guidelines. Intensive phototherapy is the first-line treatment to prevent further rise and potential kernicterus. Discontinuing breastfeeding (A) is not indicated unless there is evidence of dehydration or poor intake. IVIG (B) is used for isoimmune hemolysis, not indicated here. Ultrasound (D) is premature without evidence of cholestasis or other risk factors.
questions.hint: Consider the AAP guidelines for managing neonatal jaundice.
questions.subject: norcet-obg

questions.question: A nurse is educating a mother about newborn screening (NBS) for metabolic disorders. The mother asks, “Why does my baby need to be 24 hours old before the test?” The nurse’s BEST response is:

options.text: The test is more accurate after 24 hours because some metabolic disorders take time to manifest.
options.explanation: While some disorders take time to manifest, the primary reason is the accumulation of metabolites after protein feeding.

options.text: The test requires a full feed and adequate protein intake to detect amino acid disorders.
options.explanation: Amino acid disorders are detected by analyzing metabolites that accumulate after protein feeding, which typically occurs after 24 hours.

options.text: Early testing can cause false positives due to maternal metabolites in the bloodstream.
options.explanation: False positives due to maternal metabolites are less common than false negatives.

options.text: The state law mandates testing at 24 hours for all newborns.
options.explanation: While state laws may mandate timing, the clinical rationale is the accuracy of detection.

questions.explanation: Many metabolic disorders (e.g., PKU, MSUD) are detected by analyzing amino acids or organic acids in blood or urine. These metabolites accumulate after protein feeding, so testing before 24 hours may miss disorders or yield false negatives. False positives due to maternal metabolites (C) are less common than false negatives. While state laws may mandate timing, the clinical rationale is the accuracy of detection.
questions.hint: Consider the metabolic processes that require time to manifest after birth.
questions.subject: norcet-obg

questions.question: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate action to break the chain of infection at the portal of exit?

options.text: Wearing a surgical mask during patient care
options.explanation: Wearing a mask primarily protects the host and others from inhalation, not the portal of exit.

options.text: Covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing
options.explanation: Covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing reduces the spread of respiratory droplets, a common portal of exit for pathogens.

options.text: Administering antibiotics to a susceptible host
options.explanation: Antibiotics target the susceptible host, not the portal of exit.

options.text: Disinfecting a contaminated surface with 70% alcohol
options.explanation: Disinfecting surfaces addresses environmental contamination, not the portal of exit.

questions.explanation: Breaking the chain of infection at the portal of exit involves preventing the pathogen from leaving the host. Covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing (Option B) directly addresses this by reducing the spread of respiratory droplets, a common portal of exit for pathogens like influenza. Wearing a mask (Option A) primarily protects the host and others from inhalation, not necessarily the portal of exit. Antibiotics (Option C) target the susceptible host, not the portal of exit. Disinfecting surfaces (Option D) addresses environmental contamination, not the portal of exit.
questions.hint: Consider actions that prevent pathogens from leaving an infected host.
questions.subject: norcet-fon

questions.question: A nurse is preparing to insert a peripheral intravenous catheter. Which of the following actions BEST demonstrates the use of aseptic technique during the procedure?

options.text: Using sterile gloves without prior hand hygiene
options.explanation: Hand hygiene is essential before donning sterile gloves to prevent contamination.

options.text: Cleaning the insertion site with 70% isopropyl alcohol in a circular motion starting from the center and moving outward
options.explanation: This method follows the correct technique for skin preparation, moving from clean to dirty to reduce contamination.

options.text: Reusing a partially used sterile drape if it appears clean
options.explanation: Sterile drapes should not be reused, even if they appear clean, to maintain aseptic technique.

options.text: Wearing a sterile gown but not a mask
options.explanation: A mask is required in addition to a sterile gown to prevent contamination of the sterile field.

questions.explanation: Aseptic technique requires hand hygiene before donning gloves, using sterile equipment, cleaning the site from clean to dirty (center outward), and using sterile drapes. Option B correctly follows the recommended skin preparation technique.
questions.hint: Consider the principles of aseptic technique: hand hygiene, sterile equipment, and proper site preparation.
questions.subject: norcet-fon

questions.question: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate method to open a sterile drape without contaminating it?

options.text: Opening the drape by pulling it quickly from the wrapper to save time
options.explanation: Pulling the drape quickly can cause it to drag across non-sterile surfaces, leading to contamination.

options.text: Holding the drape at arm’s length and letting it unfold by gravity
options.explanation: Holding the drape at arm’s length does not ensure it unfolds without touching non-sterile surfaces.

options.text: Grasping the corners of the drape and lifting it straight up to allow it to unfold without touching non-sterile surfaces
options.explanation: This method ensures the drape unfolds without contacting non-sterile surfaces, maintaining sterility.

options.text: Folding the drape in half before opening to reduce bulk
options.explanation: Folding the drape can cause contamination and is not the recommended method for opening a sterile drape.

questions.explanation: The correct method involves grasping the corners and lifting vertically to allow gravity to unfold the drape without dragging it across non-sterile areas. Pulling or folding can cause contamination.
questions.hint: Think about how to unfold a sterile drape without touching non-sterile surfaces.
questions.subject: norcet-fon

questions.question: During a dressing change for a clean surgical wound, the nurse accidentally touches the sterile field with a non-sterile glove. What is the BEST immediate action?

options.text: Continue the procedure and cover the contaminated area with a new sterile drape
options.explanation: Covering the contaminated area does not address the breach in the sterile field.

options.text: Remove the contaminated glove and continue with a new sterile glove
options.explanation: Removing the contaminated glove and replacing it with a sterile one restores the sterile field.

options.text: Use an antimicrobial wipe to clean the contaminated area of the sterile field
options.explanation: Cleaning the contaminated area does not restore the sterility of the field.

options.text: Notify the physician and delay the dressing change
options.explanation: Delaying the procedure is unnecessary if the contamination is addressed immediately.

questions.explanation: Any breach of the sterile field requires immediate remediation. Removing the contaminated glove and replacing it with a sterile one maintains asepsis. Other options either do not address the contamination or are unnecessary.
questions.hint: Consider the immediate steps to restore the sterile field after contamination.
questions.subject: norcet-fon

questions.question: A student nurse is learning to set up a sterile field for a minor procedure. Which of the following actions would NOT violate the principles of aseptic technique?

options.text: Reaching over the sterile field to retrieve a missing item
options.explanation: Reaching over the sterile field can cause contamination by crossing the non-sterile zone.

options.text: Adding sterile items to the field by opening their packages and letting them drop onto the field

questions.question: A nurse needs to prepare a 0.5% sodium hypochlorite solution from a stock solution of 5%. How much stock solution should be added to 1 liter of water to achieve the desired concentration?

options.text: 50 mL
options.explanation: 50 mL would result in a 0.25% solution, not 0.5%.

options.text: 100 mL
options.explanation: 100 mL of 5% stock solution added to 1 liter of water results in a 0.5% solution.

options.text: 150 mL
options.explanation: 150 mL would result in a 0.75% solution, exceeding the desired concentration.

options.text: 200 mL
options.explanation: 200 mL would result in a 1% solution, exceeding the desired concentration.

questions.explanation: Desired concentration ÷ Stock concentration × Volume = (0.5 / 5) × 1000 mL = 0.1 × 1000 mL = 100 mL of stock solution should be added to 1 liter of water to make a 0.5% solution.
questions.hint: Use the formula: (Desired % / Stock %) × Total Volume.

questions.question: A nurse is calculating the volume of 5% sodium hypochlorite solution required to prepare 2 liters of a 0.1% disinfectant solution for environmental cleaning. How much of the 5% stock solution should be used?

options.text: 10 mL
options.explanation: 10 mL is insufficient for the desired concentration.

options.text: 40 mL
options.explanation: 40 mL of 5% sodium hypochlorite is required to prepare 2 liters of a 0.1% solution.

options.text: 50 mL
options.explanation: 50 mL would result in a higher concentration than required.

options.text: 100 mL
options.explanation: 100 mL would result in a much higher concentration than required.

questions.explanation: Desired concentration = 0.1%, Stock concentration = 5%, Total volume = 2000 mL. Volume of stock = (Desired ÷ Stock) × Total volume = (0.1 / 5) × 2000 = 0.02 × 2000 = 40 mL. Thus, 40 mL of 5% sodium hypochlorite should be diluted to 2000 mL with water to make a 0.1% solution.
questions.hint: Use the formula: (Desired concentration / Stock concentration) × Total volume.
